meta.title: The Curiosity Experiment
meta.description: Explore the psychology, neuroscience, and history of human curiosity.

intro.title: YOU WEREN’T SUPPOSED TO BE HERE.
intro.description: But now that you’re here, there’s one question worth asking.
intro.note: A QUESTION HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

opening.title: Every discovery begins with a gap.
opening.body: A question appears when what we know meets what we have yet to understand. Curiosity is the impulse that moves us toward that missing piece.
opening.prompt: What happens when you follow a question?

science.title: The mind leans toward the unknown.
science.body: Curiosity can arise when we notice a gap between what we know and what we want to know. That gap can direct attention, motivate exploration, and make new information memorable.
science.label: A useful distinction
science.detail: Dopamine participates in motivation and learning, but curiosity is not explained by one chemical or one brain region.

history.title: Questions across time
history.body: Human curiosity has taken many forms: philosophical reflection, systematic observation, experiment, and modern scientific investigation.

timeline.title: Why is there a natural order?
timeline.text: Philosophers in Greece, India, China, and elsewhere developed different ways to explain nature through reason and observation.

timeline.title: Can nature be measured?
timeline.text: Mathematical description and repeatable observation transformed the study of motion, astronomy, and physical processes.

timeline.title: How does life change over generations?
timeline.text: Charles Darwin presented a theory of evolution by natural selection, supported by extensive observations.

timeline.title: How does the brain learn?
timeline.text: Researchers combine psychology, neuroscience, computation, and behavioral experiments to study learning and curiosity.

experiment.title: Choose what you want to uncover.
experiment.body: A small question can open a much larger investigation.
experiment.question: Which mystery would you investigate first?
experiment.reveal: Curiosity turns uncertainty into a reason to explore. The next step is to ask a more precise question.
experiment.selected: Your question is a starting point—not the end.

facts.title: A few things worth wondering about

items.a: Research suggests that a curious state can improve memory for information encountered during that state, though effects depend on context and study design.
No. Curiosity can involve uncertainty or tension, especially when an important answer feels just out of reach.
Yes. Asking open questions, exploring unfamiliar ideas, and making room for uncertainty can encourage curious habits.

final.title: EVERY DISCOVERY BEGINS WITH A QUESTION.
final.body: Stay curious. Question everything. Discover more.
